questions.stem: A 62 year old retired builder has 4 years of breathlessness, wheeze and a cough most mornings. He had asthma as a child and has smoked 35 pack-years. Wheeze varies from day to day. His blood eosinophils are 0.6 ×10⁹/L. Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC is 0.58, and FEV1 rises by 14% after salbutamol but does not normalise.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Long smoking history + asthma history + eosinophilia + partial reversibility = asthma-COPD overlap. Why not Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease? Pure COPD shows minimal reversibility and no asthma history.

steps.x: Smoker with childhood asthma, eosinophilia, partial reversibility.

elim: Pure COPD shows minimal reversibility and no asthma history.
Pure asthma would normalise after bronchodilator; he has fixed obstruction too.
Causes daily purulent sputum and crackles.

steps.x: **B. Asthma-COPD overlap.** Long smoking history + asthma history + eosinophilia + partial reversibility = asthma-COPD overlap.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has persistent breathlessness, wheeze and chronic cough. Her symptoms vary from week to week and she has scattered wheeze. Spirometry shows obstruction (FEV1/FVC 0.62) that improves partly with salbutamol. Her respiratory physician suspects asthma-COPD overlap and asks about her history.
questions.q: Which combination of risk factors most supports this diagnosis?
o: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in a never-smoker
Smoking history with atopy or previous asthma
questions.e: Asthma-COPD overlap: a smoker with atopy or a prior asthma diagnosis. Why not Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency in a never-smoker? Causes early emphysema, not an overlap.

steps.x: Partly reversible obstruction; the history that links asthma and COPD.

elim: Causes early emphysema, not an overlap.

steps.x: **E. Smoking history with atopy or previous asthma.** Asthma-COPD overlap: a smoker with atopy or a prior asthma diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man with asthma-COPD overlap attends clinic. He has smoked 40 pack-years and had asthma as a teenager. He is breathless walking 100 metres and has a chronic cough with white sputum. His respiratory rate is 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. He uses his accessory muscles at rest.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Hyperinflated chest with reduced breath sounds
questions.e: Overlap shows wheeze, reduced breath sounds and hyperinflation, as in COPD. Why not Bilateral fine end-inspiratory crackles? Typical of pulmonary fibrosis.

steps.x: Mixed asthma/COPD with long smoking history.

elim: Not a feature of asthma or COPD; suggests another disease.

steps.x: **C. Hyperinflated chest with reduced breath sounds.** Overlap shows wheeze, reduced breath sounds and hyperinflation, as in COPD.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has had asthma-COPD overlap for 10 years and still smokes. In the last year she has had four courses of steroids and antibiotics and one hospital admission. She asks what she is most at risk of.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication of her condition?
questions.e: Overlap complications: frequent exacerbations, respiratory failure and reduced lung function. Why not Lung abscess? Not a typical complication.

clues: four courses of steroids and antibiotics
steps.x: Overlap, still smoking, repeated attacks.

elim: Linked to asbestos, not this condition.

steps.x: **A. Frequent exacerbations and respiratory failure.** Overlap complications: frequent exacerbations, respiratory failure and reduced lung function.

questions.stem: A 55 year old woman with a 30 pack-year smoking history has breathlessness and wheeze. She had eczema and asthma in childhood. Her wheeze varies and she has a chronic morning cough. Her GP wants to know which spirometry result would best fit asthma-COPD overlap.
questions.q: Which is the most likely spirometry result?
questions.e: Overlap: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 with partial reversibility. Why not FEV1/FVC 0.6 with no reversibility? Fits pure COPD.

steps.x: Smoker with childhood asthma and eczema.
**C. FEV1/FVC 0.6 with partial reversibility.** Overlap: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 with partial reversibility.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man was told he had COPD 3 years ago. He had hay fever and asthma as a child and has smoked 25 pack-years. His symptoms vary from week to week. Blood eosinophils are 0.7 ×10⁹/L and his FEV1 rises by 16% after salbutamol, with FEV1/FVC staying below 0.7.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Partially reversible obstruction with asthma features = overlap. Why not Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease? Pure COPD does not show this much reversibility or eosinophilia.

clues: hay fever and asthma as a child
steps.x: COPD label, but atopy, variability, eosinophilia and partial reversibility.

elim: Pure COPD does not show this much reversibility or eosinophilia.
Causes orthopnoea and oedema, not reversible obstruction.

steps.x: **B. Asthma-COPD overlap.** Partially reversible obstruction with asthma features = overlap.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has a chronic cough and breathlessness. She has smoked since 16. She was treated for asthma at school. She has episodic wheeze that wakes her at night, and her chest is hyperinflated with reduced breath sounds.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A mixed asthma/COPD picture in a smoker with prior asthma = overlap. Why not Asthma? Her heavy smoking, chronic cough and hyperinflation add a COPD picture.

steps.x: Mixed asthma and COPD features in a smoker.

elim: Her heavy smoking, chronic cough and hyperinflation add a COPD picture.
Daily purulent sputum and coarse crackles.
No weight loss, haemoptysis or focal signs.

steps.x: **B. Asthma-COPD overlap.** A mixed asthma/COPD picture in a smoker with prior asthma = overlap.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with asthma-COPD overlap has yearly spirometry. His FEV1 has fallen by about 90 mL each year, faster than expected for either asthma or COPD alone. He continues to smoke 15 cigarettes a day and has had two exacerbations in the last year. His inhaler technique is good.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication shown by these results?
questions.e: Overlap causes reduced lung function with faster decline. Why not Development of pulmonary fibrosis? Would cause restriction, not falling FEV1 in obstruction.

clues: faster than expected for either asthma or COPD alone
steps.x: FEV1 falling faster than either disease alone.

elim: Would cause restriction, not falling FEV1 in obstruction.
A consistent yearly decline is real.
Not a cause of falling FEV1.

steps.x: **A. Accelerated decline in lung function.** Overlap causes reduced lung function with faster decline.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman with a 40 pack-year smoking history has breathlessness, chronic cough and wheeze. Spirometry shows fixed airflow obstruction with FEV1/FVC 0.6. She had hay fever as a child. Her doctor is considering whether she has asthma-COPD overlap rather than COPD alone.
questions.q: Which finding would most support asthma-COPD overlap?
questions.e: Eosinophilia, asthma history and partial reversibility suggest overlap. Why not Alpha-1 antitrypsin level low? Suggests AAT deficiency emphysema.

steps.x: Smoker with fixed obstruction; looking for an asthma component.

elim: A COPD complication, not an asthma feature.

steps.x: **C. High blood eosinophil count.** Eosinophilia, asthma history and partial reversibility suggest overlap.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with asthma-COPD overlap, mainly COPD, has 3 days of worsening breathlessness. He is drowsy. Arterial blood gas on air shows pH 7.29, PaO2 7.1 kPa, PaCO2 8.2 kPa and HCO3- 33 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Acute on chronic type 2 respiratory failure in overlap
questions.e: Overlap can cause respiratory failure; raised bicarbonate shows a chronic component. Why not Type 1 respiratory failure in overlap? His PaCO2 is raised.

steps.x: Drowsy, acidotic, raised CO2 and bicarbonate.

elim: The pH is low, so it is not compensated.

steps.x: **A. Acute on chronic type 2 respiratory failure in overlap.** Overlap can cause respiratory failure; raised bicarbonate shows a chronic component.

questions.stem: A 56 year old cleaner has 3 years of breathlessness on exertion, wheeze and a productive morning cough. She has smoked 30 pack-years and had asthma as a child. Her chest is hyperinflated with scattered wheeze. Spirometry shows partially reversible obstruction, with FEV1/FVC 0.61 after salbutamol.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Smoking with an asthma background and partial reversibility = overlap. Why not Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease? Pure COPD has minimal reversibility and no asthma history.

steps.x: Smoker + childhood asthma + partially reversible obstruction.

elim: Pure COPD has minimal reversibility and no asthma history.

steps.x: **A. Asthma-COPD overlap.** Smoking with an asthma background and partial reversibility = overlap.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with childhood asthma who has smoked 30 pack-years has 2 years of breathlessness and cough. His GP suspects asthma-COPD overlap and wants to confirm the diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Spirometry: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 with partial reversibility. Why not Chest X-ray? May show hyperinflation but cannot confirm the diagnosis.

steps.x: Suspected overlap needs obstruction and its reversibility shown.

elim: May show hyperinflation but cannot confirm the diagnosis.
Shows emphysema but does not show reversibility.
Supports asthma but does not show fixed obstruction.

steps.x: **E. Spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility.** Spirometry: FEV1/FVC below 0.7 with partial reversibility.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with a long smoking history and previous asthma has variable breathlessness and wheeze. Spirometry is booked for 6 weeks' time. Her GP wants first-line tests to look for an asthma component now.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Peak flow diary and blood eosinophils
questions.e: First-line in overlap: peak flow variability and blood eosinophils. Why not Arterial blood gas? For acute or severe disease.

steps.x: Looking for variability and eosinophilic inflammation before spirometry.
**D. Peak flow diary and blood eosinophils.** First-line in overlap: peak flow variability and blood eosinophils.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has 3 years of breathlessness, wheeze and a chronic cough. He has smoked 40 pack-years and had asthma until age 20. His blood eosinophils are raised. He has spirometry before and after salbutamol in the respiratory clinic.
questions.q: Which result is most consistent with asthma-COPD overlap?
questions.e: Overlap: obstruction stays below 0.7 but improves partly after bronchodilator. Why not FEV1/FVC 0.56 rising to 0.57, FEV1 up 2%? Minimal reversibility: pure COPD.

steps.x: Smoker with asthma history: expect partial reversibility.
**B. FEV1/FVC 0.56 rising to 0.62, FEV1 up 13%.** Overlap: obstruction stays below 0.7 but improves partly after bronchodilator.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman is diagnosed with asthma-COPD overlap. She has stopped smoking and uses salbutamol several times a day. Her FEV1 rose by 14% after salbutamol. Her respiratory nurse wants a blood test that will help predict whether an inhaled corticosteroid will help.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Eosinophilia predicts a good ICS response, as in eosinophilic asthma. Why not Total IgE? Shows atopy; eosinophils better predict ICS response.

clues: predict whether an inhaled corticosteroid will help
steps.x: Predicting ICS response.

elim: Shows atopy; eosinophils better predict ICS response.

steps.x: **C. Full blood count for eosinophils.** Eosinophilia predicts a good ICS response, as in eosinophilic asthma.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has breathlessness and wheeze. He has smoked 20 a day since 18 and had asthma as a child. His peak flow varies by 18% over 2 weeks. The respiratory team want the test that will separate overlap from pure COPD.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Spirometry: partial reversibility in overlap, minimal in COPD. Why not Chest X-ray? Cannot measure reversibility.

steps.x: Need to show partially reversible obstruction.

elim: Shows eosinophils but not airflow obstruction.

steps.x: **D. Spirometry with reversibility testing.** Spirometry: partial reversibility in overlap, minimal in COPD.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man who has smoked 30 pack-years and had childhood asthma keeps a twice-daily peak flow diary for 2 weeks. His morning readings are much lower than his evening readings.

visual.title: Peak flow diary
visual.caption: Marked diurnal variation on a low baseline.

questions.q: Which finding would most support asthma-COPD overlap over pure COPD?
o: Rising peak flow over the 2 weeks only
questions.e: Variable peak flow shows the asthma component of overlap. Why not Constant low peak flow? Fixed obstruction fits COPD.

steps.x: Morning dips in a smoker with asthma history.
**D. Peak flow variability over 20%.** Variable peak flow shows the asthma component of overlap.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman is newly diagnosed with asthma-COPD overlap. She uses salbutamol several times a day. Her blood eosinophils are 0.5 ×10⁹/L. She has stopped smoking and her FEV1/FVC is 0.63 with partial reversibility. She has no other illnesses.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial maintenance treatment?
questions.e: Start ICS (e.g. beclometasone) early, combined with a long-acting bronchodilator. Why not LABA alone? LABA without ICS is unsafe with an asthma component.

steps.x: Overlap needs early ICS with a long-acting bronchodilator.

elim: LABA without ICS is unsafe with an asthma component.

steps.x: **A. ICS with a long-acting bronchodilator.** Start ICS (e.g. beclometasone) early, combined with a long-acting bronchodilator.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with asthma-COPD overlap uses an inhaled corticosteroid alone with good technique. He remains breathless on exertion and uses salbutamol daily. He stopped smoking a year ago. His oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Increase ICS to high dose alone
questions.e: Add bronchodilators: LABA, with or without LAMA. Why not Add oral prednisolone? Not maintenance therapy.

steps.x: On ICS alone, still breathless.

elim: Bronchodilators are needed for the COPD component.
For frequent exacerbations after inhalers are optimised.

steps.x: **A. Add a LABA.** Add bronchodilators: LABA, with or without LAMA.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman with asthma-COPD overlap takes an ICS/LABA inhaler with good technique and adherence. She has had three exacerbations this year and is breathless walking on the flat. She stopped smoking 2 years ago and has completed pulmonary rehabilitation.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
o: Stop ICS because of pneumonia risk
Triple therapy with ICS, LABA and LAMA
questions.e: Triple therapy (ICS + LABA + LAMA) is the definitive inhaled treatment. Why not Change to LAMA alone? Removes the ICS needed for the asthma component.

steps.x: Uncontrolled on ICS/LABA.

elim: Removes the ICS needed for the asthma component.

steps.x: **E. Triple therapy with ICS, LABA and LAMA.** Triple therapy (ICS + LABA + LAMA) is the definitive inhaled treatment.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with asthma-COPD overlap still smokes 15 cigarettes a day. He is on triple inhaled therapy with good technique and his oxygen saturation is 95% breathing air. He asks what else would most help his long-term outlook.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate intervention?
questions.e: Smoking cessation and pulmonary rehabilitation matter throughout. Why not Home nebuliser? Not first in long-term care.

steps.x: Still smoking on maximal inhalers.

elim: Only if hypoxaemic, and he must stop smoking first.

steps.x: **E. Smoking cessation support.** Smoking cessation and pulmonary rehabilitation matter throughout.

questions.stem: A 65 year old woman with asthma-COPD overlap has stopped smoking and takes triple therapy. She is limited by breathlessness after 100 metres and has become housebound and deconditioned. Her oxygen saturation is 93% breathing air and she has not had an exacerbation for 6 months.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next intervention?
questions.e: Pulmonary rehabilitation is important throughout overlap care. Why not Bronchial thermoplasty? For selected severe asthma only.

steps.x: Breathless, deconditioned, already on maximal inhalers, not smoking.

elim: She is already on triple therapy.

steps.x: **E. Pulmonary rehabilitation.** Pulmonary rehabilitation is important throughout overlap care.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with asthma-COPD overlap, mainly COPD, has 3 days of worsening breathlessness and green sputum. His oxygen saturation is 84% breathing air. His respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute. Previous blood gases showed CO2 retention.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate oxygen therapy?
questions.e: Exacerbations: controlled oxygen if COPD dominant, plus bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics if needed. Why not 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask? Uncontrolled oxygen risks worsening hypercapnia.

steps.x: COPD-dominant overlap with previous CO2 retention.

elim: He is hypoxic and needs oxygen now.
Too high for a CO2 retainer.

steps.x: **B. 28% Venturi mask, target 88-92%.** Exacerbations: controlled oxygen if COPD dominant, plus bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics if needed.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with asthma-COPD overlap has 2 days of worsening wheeze and breathlessness and green sputum. Her temperature is 37.9°C, oxygen saturation 90% breathing air and respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute. She is not allergic to penicillin.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics
questions.e: Exacerbation: oxygen, bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics if infection. Why not Nebulised bronchodilators alone? She also needs steroids and antibiotics for purulent sputum.

steps.x: Exacerbation with infection signs.

elim: She also needs steroids and antibiotics for purulent sputum.

steps.x: **C. Nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics.** Exacerbation: oxygen, bronchodilators, steroids, antibiotics if infection.

questions.stem: A 56 year old man with asthma-COPD overlap has blood eosinophils of 0.9 ×10⁹/L. He is on a LAMA alone and has had two exacerbations this year. He no longer smokes. His inhaler technique is good and his FEV1 rises by 15% after salbutamol.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate change to his treatment?
questions.e: Overlap needs ICS early; eosinophilia predicts a good response. Why not Add a second LAMA? Two LAMAs are never combined.

steps.x: High eosinophils, no ICS, exacerbations.

elim: Inhaled therapy must be optimised first.

steps.x: **B. Add an inhaled corticosteroid.** Overlap needs ICS early; eosinophilia predicts a good response.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman with asthma-COPD overlap takes part in a research study and has a bronchial biopsy and sputum analysis. She had childhood asthma and has smoked 35 pack-years. Her FEV1 improves partly after salbutamol.
questions.q: Which is the most likely pattern of inflammation?
questions.e: Overlap combines eosinophilic asthma-type and neutrophilic COPD-type inflammation. Why not Granulomatous inflammation? Seen in sarcoidosis and TB.

steps.x: Asthma background plus smoking.
**C. Mixed eosinophilic and neutrophilic inflammation.** Overlap combines eosinophilic asthma-type and neutrophilic COPD-type inflammation.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with asthma-COPD overlap asks why his breathing improves a little with his salbutamol inhaler but never returns to normal. His FEV1 rose by 14% after salbutamol but FEV1/FVC stayed at 0.61. He has smoked 30 pack-years.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Reversible bronchospasm plus fixed structural damage
questions.e: Part of the narrowing is reversible (asthma), part fixed (COPD). Why not Inhaler technique error? Would reduce benefit altogether.

steps.x: Partial improvement but never normal.

elim: Would show restriction and no response.
Would return to normal, as in asthma.
Not the cause of partial reversibility.

steps.x: **D. Reversible bronchospasm plus fixed structural damage.** Part of the narrowing is reversible (asthma), part fixed (COPD).

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with asthma-COPD overlap has blood eosinophils of 0.8 ×10⁹/L. She has stopped smoking. After 3 months of an ICS/LABA inhaler her exacerbations stop and her FEV1 improves by 200 mL.
questions.q: Which is the most likely reason for her good response?
questions.e: Eosinophilia predicts a good ICS response, like eosinophilic asthma. Why not Bronchodilator effect of the ICS? ICS are anti-inflammatory, not bronchodilators.

steps.x: High eosinophils, good ICS response.
**E. Steroid-sensitive eosinophilic inflammation.** Eosinophilia predicts a good ICS response, like eosinophilic asthma.

questions.stem: A 53 year old woman has had asthma since childhood and has smoked 20 a day for 30 years. Her FEV1 has fallen faster than her non-smoking asthmatic sister's and faster than her smoking brother's with COPD.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her rapid decline?
o: Remodelling from both asthma and COPD processes
questions.e: Long-standing inflammation and remodelling from both processes accelerate decline. Why not Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency? Would affect the siblings too.

clues: faster than her non-smoking asthmatic sister's
steps.x: Decline faster than either disease alone.

elim: A consistent faster decline is real.

steps.x: **D. Remodelling from both asthma and COPD processes.** Long-standing inflammation and remodelling from both processes accelerate decline.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man with asthma-COPD overlap has a CT chest showing centrilobular emphysema. He also has bronchial wall thickening and raised sputum eosinophils. He had asthma as a child and has smoked 45 pack-years.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation of these combined findings?
o: Smoking damage on an atopic asthma background
questions.e: Overlap: COPD-type structural damage plus asthma-type eosinophilic inflammation. Why not Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency? Causes panlobular basal emphysema without eosinophilia.

steps.x: Emphysema plus eosinophilic airway inflammation.

elim: Causes panlobular basal emphysema without eosinophilia.

steps.x: **E. Smoking damage on an atopic asthma background.** Overlap: COPD-type structural damage plus asthma-type eosinophilic inflammation.
